title: Saritha Komatireddy Challenges Letitia James for New York Attorney General
excerpt: The first South Asian major-party nominee for statewide office in New York is taking on one of the state's most powerful Democrats — and the polls are tightening ahead of the November 3 election.
body:
• Republican Saritha Komatireddy is challenging Democratic Attorney General Letitia James in New York's November 3 statewide election — the first South Asian major-party nominee for statewide office in New York history.
  • Born in Brooklyn to parents who emigrated from India in the 1980s, Komatireddy is a former federal terrorism prosecutor and a former clerk to Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh; she was nominated by President Trump to be a federal judge and told NY1 she had also worked for the DEA administrator under President Biden.
  • A Siena poll conducted September 11-17 put James at 52 per cent and Komatireddy at 39 per cent — but the gap narrowed from an 18-point James lead in August.
  • For New York readers: the attorney general race is statewide, so every registered New York voter gets this race on their November 3 ballot. A Komatireddy win would make her the first Indian American elected to statewide office in New York.

A historic first on the statewide ballot

In New York, Republican Saritha Komatireddy is taking on one of the most powerful Democrats in the state — Attorney General Letitia James. Komatireddy is the first South Asian major-party nominee for statewide office in New York, a milestone that has put the race on the radar of Indian American communities well beyond the state's borders.

President Donald Trump endorsed her in August, and the race has tightened: the Siena poll's 13-point margin in mid-September was down from James's 18-point lead a month earlier, according to IANS.

From Brooklyn to the federal bench shortlist

Komatireddy was born in Brooklyn to parents who came from India in the 1980s. Her legal résumé runs through some of the most visible posts in American law: she clerked for Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh and served as a federal terrorism prosecutor. "I worked for the DEA administrator while Joe Biden was president… I was nominated to be a federal judge by President Trump," she told NY1 in August.

"You can work hard, dream big, and have a shot at achieving those dreams."

— Saritha Komatireddy, speaking about her parents to NY1

Context & Background

Her candidacy sits inside a wider wave: Indian American candidates are chasing a string of firsts in the November 3 elections across at least five states, from Nithya Raman's bid for Los Angeles mayor to a possible first Hindu in the Texas Legislature and Amar Mukunda's near-certain state Senate seat in Maryland, IANS reports. It follows recent milestones including Zohran Mamdani becoming New York City's first Indian American mayor last year.

The backdrop is complicated. Komatireddy is running as a Republican at a moment when parts of her own party are turning against the H-1B visa programme — the pathway long used by Indian professionals. Vice President JD Vance said last week that most H-1B holders were being used to replace American workers, the Trump administration has imposed a $100,000 fee on certain H-1B petitions (since blocked by a second federal judge), and the employment green-card route for eight technology firms has been suspended, according to a second IANS report. She is one of at least nine Indian American Republicans on the November 3 ballot.

Impact & Analysis

The attorney general's office in New York is no ceremonial post — it has been a national-stage office under James, whose tenure has included high-profile cases against major corporations and Trump himself. A Republican win would flip one of the Democrats' most prominent statewide offices and hand the GOP a proof of concept: an Indian American woman carrying a diverse, deep-blue state.

Even in defeat, the candidacy moves the representation needle. Indian American Impact counts more than 250 Indian Americans in elected office nationwide, a number that has grown steadily since Kumar Barve became the first Indian American elected to any state legislature in 1990. A statewide nomination in New York — the state with one of the country's largest South Asian populations — is itself the historic first, whatever the November 3 result.

What's Next

The general election is on November 3. Polling suggests James remains the favourite, but the narrowing gap means this race bears watching through October. For Indian American voters in New York, the question is whether community turnout can make history in a statewide race for the first time.
